nameStory: The 'twayblade' name comes from the plant's distinctive pair of leaves - 'tway' is an old English word meaning 'two.' The 'broad-lipped' part refers to the unusually wide lower petal of its tiny orchid flowers, which flares out like a landing pad for visiting insects.
description: Broad-lipped twayblade is a small, delicate orchid that's easy to overlook in the forest understory. It grows just 4-8 inches tall with a single stem topped by a spike of tiny yellowish-green flowers. The plant's most recognizable feature is its pair of broad, oval leaves that sit about halfway up the stem, looking almost like they're cupping the flower spike above them.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two broad, oval leaves positioned opposite each other halfway up the stem, with a soft, slightly waxy texture and prominent parallel veins running lengthwise

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green orchid flowers arranged in a loose spike, each with a distinctively broad, flared lower lip that's wider than it is long

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single unbranched stem rising 4-8 inches from the ground, often growing in small scattered groups rather than dense clusters

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, pale green stem that feels slightly succulent and fleshy to the touch, with no leaves except for the distinctive pair

habitat: Look for broad-lipped twayblade in cool, moist coniferous and mixed forests, especially under spruce and fir trees. It prefers acidic, humus-rich soils and is often found in mossy areas or near rotting logs in shaded woodland settings throughout New England's mountains and cooler regions.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge in late spring, with the characteristic pair of leaves unfurling as the stem grows. Plants are easiest to spot once the leaves are fully developed.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs in early to mid-summer, when the tiny orchid blooms are most visible. This is the prime identification season when all features are present.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to yellow and die back, becoming much harder to locate as they blend with fallen leaves and forest debris.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain visible; the plant persists underground via its root system until the following spring.

funFact: Despite being an orchid, broad-lipped twayblade is partially parasitic - it gets some of its nutrients by tapping into underground fungal networks that connect forest trees, essentially 'stealing' sugars that the fungi are trading with tree roots!
confusionNotes: The two-leaf arrangement might remind you of other woodland plants like wild ginger or trout lily, but those have much larger leaves and completely different flowers. Remember: if you see two broad leaves halfway up a short stem with tiny greenish flowers above, you've likely found a twayblade orchid.
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently moved from the genus Listera to Neottia based on DNA studies, so older field guides may still list it under its former scientific name Listera convallarioides. Many botanists and naturalists still use both names interchangeably.
compareHints: Broad-lipped twayblade is distinguished from its twayblade relatives by its wider flower lip and broader leaves. Southern twayblade has much narrower leaves, while heartleaf twayblade has distinctly heart-shaped leaves rather than oval ones. The broad, flared lip of the flowers is your best bet for confirming this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's twayblades, Southern Twayblade is distinguished by its deeply split flower lip and preference for acidic coniferous forests.

Heartleaf Twayblade is the only Neottia species in New England with heart-shaped leaves - its relatives like Southern Twayblade have oval leaves, while Broad-lipped Twayblade has broader, more rounded leaves.
Among its twayblade relatives, Auricled Twayblade is distinguished by its yellowish-green flowers with the characteristic ear-like projections on the lip petal.
